newsitem.title: FRANCE: France wants to improve integration of immigrants.
newsitem.headline: France wants to improve integration of immigrants.

text.p: France's centre-right government, assailed by the left and extreme right over the explosive immigration issue, announced measures on Wednesday to hasten integration of legal immigrants into mainstream society.

"The unfavourable economic context, marked by unemployment, has had negative effects on integration (of immigrants)...and aggravated tensions with native-born French people," Territorial Planning, Urban Affairs and Integration Minister Jean-Claude Gaudin told a news conference.

He spoke after Eric Raoult, junior minister for Urban Affairs and Integration, presented to the weekly cabinet meeting 18 steps designed to help 3.5 to four million foreign nationals and up to 1.7 million of their French-born children better adapt to France.

The measures include free tuition in speaking French, help in homework for children of non-French speaking parents, aid in finding jobs and cutting down the time needed for naturalisation, seen as the key to integration. President Jacques Chirac wants to cut the time to a minimum six years instead of seven.
There were also moves to close some hostels for single foreign workers, which police say are sometimes hotbeds of Islamic militancy or centres for drug trafficking.
Chirac told the cabinet the measures could only be taken if the government simultaneously cracked down hard against illegal immigrants who officials say number hundreds of thousands.

The new measures, estimated to cost 3.5 billion francs ($620 million), came as the Senate gave final approval to a controversial bill to clamp down on illegal immigration which had prompted widespread protests by artists, intellectuals and leftist parties.
Left-wing parties pledged to appeal against the bill, which now becomes law, to the Constitutional Council.
Socialist senator Guy Allouche accused the centre-right government of pushing the bill through for party political ends, with an eye to luring voters away from the far-right National Front.

The bill introduces articles to immigration regulations that will allow police to keep the passports or travel documents of illegal immigrants, who authorities say often destroy their documents when caught in order to avoid being sent home.
Gaudin said the measures announced on Wednesday to better integrate legal arrivals were also aimed at checking the rising power of the FN which wants to expel all foreigners from France.
"The tensions caused (by difficulties in integrating immigrants) are feeding the speeches of hate and exclusion of a racist and xenophobic party," he said.
"And we don't need lessons from the Left, whose suggestions of giving foreigners the right to vote only automatically produce more backers for the FN," he said.

The FN, which opinion polls indicate can count on the votes of about 15 percent of the population, has seen its fortunes rise in the past decade parallel with unemployment, now at nearly 13 percent, and changes in immigration patterns.
Immigrants once came mostly from nearby European countries such as Spain, Italy, Portugal and Poland, whose descendants Gaudin said made up nearly a fifth of today's French population.
Current immigration is mostly from Africa and Asia, including many Moslems whose lifestyles often clash with those of secular French society at large.
"We reject racism but we also reject the voluntary existence of self-enclosed communities," he said.
